items.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007
items.q: My great grandmother, through various family connections, knew the family of Henry David Thoreau. And in fact my great great grandmother boarded with the Thoreaus.

ctx.x: There’s a lot of stuff floating around.

Is there? Well it’s interesting. Yeah, one of the hanging judges, Samuel Sewall of the Bay Colony was one of my ancestors and he’s famous for being the hanging judge of course. But the important thing, one of the important things about him in addition to that was that he wrote the first anti-slavery tract produced in the United States. He wrote, his principle was I just do not see how God is differentiating between blacks and whites, they were all human and therefore slavery should not exist. That was his…

had not broken that up Thoreau would not have been able to build a cabin on a lake in Massachusetts, which of course produced the famous Walden. So that’s the second great book that the family created by inadvertence. There’s a third one actually. My grandmother’s cousin, I believe that’s the connection, Abigail May, married a lunatic, Bronson Alcott, who was responsible for creating a utopian colony called Fruitlands. And of course they scorned money and so nobody ever had any money and it was all a dreadful…
